Second. Hey, what has he become like?
First. Hey, don't you know? The Bhattacharya had not yet got out of bed, when this one suddenly came up to the door of the bedroom. Then a boy student says: "Bhattacharya, Bhattacharya! Get up, get up! That sannyasi has come." Then the Bhattacharya — thump! — jumped up and fell at his feet. And he put Jagannatha's rice prasada into his hand and says: "Eat!" And our master, like a madman, without thinking, swallowed that rice in a flash — without bathing, without even rinsing his mouth! And having swallowed it, like a madman, he broke out in gooseflesh all over, his clothes got soaked with tears, his throat is gurgling — and he's rolling on the ground as if he'd had a fit. What will happen, we don't know.
Gopinatha Acharya (having listened). Mukunda, did you hear?
Mukunda. It is because of your grief that the Lord resolved on this.
Servants. Let's go and look for Gopinatha Acharya. (Exeunt.)
Gopinatha Acharya. Good, good that they did not notice me. Let us wait here for Damodara and Jagadananda. (They do so.)
(Enter Damodara, acting amazement.)
Damodara.
notes: The bala-bhoga is the early morning meal of Jagannatha; the Hari-vallabha is the next offering.
The sentence in square brackets is found only in the Kāvyamālā; without it the following speech of "Both" (Damodara and Jagadananda) hangs in the air in GGM.
The servants speak a vulgar Prakrit (Magadhi: ale for are, bhaṭṭācālia and so on).

verses_en.text:
Without a pen the Lord has bound the mighty wild elephant intoxicated with rut;
without sprinkling water He has as it were quenched the flame of His own people's burning heart —
for He, as if by chance, has made the heart of this lord of pandits,
harder than a thunderbolt, juicy as nectar.*
Gopinatha Acharya (approaching). Damodara, what is this?
Damodara. It is a secret; we shall tell it. But I have come here for your sake. Let us go out by another door and follow the Lord, who has already returned to His lodging.
(All three walk a few steps. Damodara, having recited the verse "Without a pen…", tells everything.)
Gopinatha Acharya. I have already heard everything from the lips of those two servants who were talking together.
Damodara. It is only by your mercy that this good fortune has fallen to him. Come, let us go quickly to the Lord. For the Bhattacharya too, having performed his daily rites, will soon come there; then it will become clear what is in his heart. So far not a word has been said.
(They walk about the stage.)
(Enter the Lord, already seated in His place, Nityananda and Jagadananda.)
The Lord. Jagadananda, where is Gopinatha Acharya?
Jagadananda. Here, here the Acharya is hurrying with Damodara and Mukunda.
Gopinatha Acharya (approaching). Glory, glory to the all-merciful One!
Jagadananda. Ah, what is this play of words of yours, never heard before?
Gopinatha Acharya. That is known only to the Lord.* (Approaches and bows.)
Behind the scenes. Master! This is not the road to the temple of Sri Jagannatha!
The Lord (having listened). Acharya, find out what is there.
Gopinatha Acharya (looking towards the back of the stage). I see, I see! Here is the Bhattacharya, not even having seen Sri Jagannatha, coming to fall at the Lord's feet.
Damodara. That was known beforehand.
(All stand looking into his face. Enter Sarvabhauma, his mind opened by amazement.)
Sarvabhauma (to himself). Ah, Gopinatha Acharya spoke the truth. If even our heart has become like this, then He is God Himself. (Walks about the stage with longing.) Ah, here is my maternal aunt's house. Let me enter. (Acts entering.)
(The Acharya rises and goes out to meet him.)
Sarvabhauma (looking ahead). Acharya, what is Svami doing?
Acharya. This way, this way, please, sir.
Sarvabhauma (approaching, he prostrates himself like a rod before the Lord and joins his palms).
notes: Vārī, a pen or post for catching elephants. The Kāvyamālā notes here the figure nidarśanā.
So in GGM (bhagavatām); the Kāvyamālā has bhavatām, "that is known only to you [yourselves]".

verses_en.text:
When the Lord, overcome by the rasa of various pastimes, plays His play like a man,
even seeing Him face to face one does not grasp His truth:
ah, a man cannot recognise the philosopher's stone by sight
until by its touch it turns mere iron into gold.
And further:

Abode of the hearts of Your own, O Lord, master of Padma,*
You, Padmanabha, wander the earth in the guise of a king of ascetics.
How can we, like beasts, perceive You, all-powerful, though manifest?
Alas, fate is hostile to us!
The Lord (covering His ears). Bhattacharya, I am only an object of your fatherly affection. Why do you say such things? (To Himself.) Ah, now I must test what is in his heart. (Aloud.) O great soul, explain, then: what is the meaning of the shastras?
Bhattacharya (joining his palms). Master!
notes: Padma is Lakshmi; Padmanabha, "lotus-navelled", is Vishnu.

verses_en.text:
The shastras, though full of different views, are so composed, each according to its own taste;
otherwise how would their experts be skilled in refuting one another?
But the supreme aim in them is something special: the unselfish bhakti-yoga of Murari,
and it is obtained only by the mercy of the Lord.
And further:

The Vedas, the Puranas, the Bhārata, the tantras and mantras — all of them
teach that the reality is Brahman alone; but in its truth all go astray.
For —

Its primary meaning, from [the root meaning] "being great" and "making great",* is the possession of attributes;
and those who proclaim it attributeless are unable to prove it.
So it is said in the Hayaśīrṣa-pañcarātra:
notes: The word brahman is derived from the root bṛh, "to grow, to be great": bṛhattva, "greatness", and bṛṁhaṇatva, "the power of making great".

verses_en.text:
Every shruti that speaks of the attributeless in fact names the one possessed of attributes;
and when they are examined, the one possessed of attributes, ah, for the most part proves the stronger.
For look: from the shruti "From bliss indeed these beings are born, by bliss, once born, they live, into bliss they go and enter"* it follows that it possesses attributes, since it stands in the [case-]roles of source, instrument, object and the rest. So too from the words "That from which these beings are born…",* and in the sayings "It saw…" and "He desired…"* — where "seeing" is deliberation and "desire" is resolve — from these two too the possession of attributes follows; so attributelessness cannot be established. And once attributes are established, form too follows from the attributes. And this form is not material, for [in the Brahma-sūtras] "light" and "foot" are spoken of:* as the non-materiality of the light is proved, so too is the non-materiality of this form. If it were merely attributeless, the way would be opened to the doctrine of the void. Therefore the word "Brahman" is used in its primary sense, and in the primary sense Brahman is Bhagavan — that is what remains [in the end]. As it is said:
The knowers of the truth call that non-dual knowledge the truth,
which is named Brahman, Paramatma and Bhagavan.*
But those who are possessed by the demon of defending their own side and, although the primary meaning is by no means absent, proclaim through a secondary meaning* an attributelessness that can never be defined — theirs is mere obstinacy. In reality:
notes: Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.6.
Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1.
Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3 (tad aikṣata); Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6 (so 'kāmayata).
Cf. Brahma-sūtra 1.1.24 (jyotiś caraṇābhidhānāt), where "light" is interpreted as Brahman on the ground of the mention of its "feet" (quarters).
Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.2.11. In the Kāvyamālā the verse is quoted only in part and unnumbered; in GGM in full, also unnumbered.

Lakṣaṇā, the secondary (figurative) meaning of a word, to which the Advaitins resort in interpreting brahman as attributeless. The construction mukhyārthābhāvābhāve 'pi is understood as "although there is no absence of the primary meaning": by the rules of poetics lakṣaṇā is resorted to only when the primary meaning is impossible, while here it is quite possible. M. Guha's Bengali translation renders the passage more freely ("both in the absence of the primary meaning and being unable to define it even by the secondary meaning"), but the general sense — a reproach of forced interpretation — is the same.

verses_en.text:
Bliss is said to be twofold: embodied and unembodied.
The refuge of the unembodied is the embodied; the embodied bliss is Achyuta.

The unembodied is the Paramatma, whose nature is knowledge, devoid of gunas,
self-existent, unchanging — and that is Brahman: such is the view of the saints.

When the truth is examined there is no difference between the unembodied and the embodied:
the difference is only conceived by the Vedas — as between a gem and its radiance.
So in the Hayaśīrṣa-pañcarātra. And in the Kapila-pañcarātra too, the words of Kapila addressed to Agastya:

Two Brahmans are to be known — the embodied and the unembodied;
the all-pervading Narayana, by nature embodied and unembodied, is the object of meditation.*
Only the doctrine of the Pancharatra is free from partisanship. But the adherents of the doctrine of a purely attributeless Brahman, defining Brahman as unembodied bliss alone, reveal only the coarseness of their impressions,* but cannot establish attributelessness. But if the doctrine of the Pancharatra is accepted, both the sayings "Bliss is the form of Brahman" and "Brahman is one without a second"* are established: embodiment by [bliss being called] form, and non-duality by the comparison "as a gem and its radiance". Therefore that Bhagavan is Brahman is the view of all the shastras. Some, however, owing to the peculiarity of their impressions, thinking that in Bhagavan — embodied bliss — the form is merely assumed for the sake of play, say that Brahman is only unembodied bliss. But the followers of the Pancharatra are faultless śiṣṭas,* for they worship Bhagavan; therefore it is by their conduct that the meaning of the Vedas is to be inferred. For —
notes: Verses 38–41 are unnumbered in GGM (there 42 follows straight after 37); the numbers follow the Kāvyamālā. The Hayaśīrṣa- and Kapila-pañcarātra are Vaishnava agamas. Verse 37 is quoted in the Chaitanya-charitamrita (Madhya 6.142).
Vāsanā, subconscious impressions, tendencies left over from past experience.
The first saying is attributed to the shruti (in GGM it is marked as Chāndogya 6.2.1, which applies only to the second: ekam evādvitīyam).
A śiṣṭa is a recognised authority on conduct, a "well-bred" person whose conduct serves as a source of dharma.

verses_en.text:
The branches of the tree of the Vedas are thousands; it is not all open to direct perception:
its parts are to be inferred from the words of the Puranas and the conduct of the faultless śiṣṭas.
Here are words of the Puranas, for example: "…whose friend is the supreme bliss, the full, eternal Brahman"* and so on. "Full", because possessed of form; the attributeless Brahman is not full, that is, devoid of form. And the śiṣṭas are the Sattvatas.* Their doctrine is this: "The supreme deity is Vasudeva; from Vasudeva, the supreme Soul, comes Sankarshana, the 'jiva'" and so on. "Jiva" here is the one who enlivens, who creates the jivas, not a jiva himself. And He is the Atman, for [the Lord] Himself said: "The Brahman of sound and the supreme Brahman are both My eternal bodies."* So from Him the creation of the jivas proceeds. Thus the meaning of the shastras is that the embodied bliss is Krishna.
The Lord. Splendid, splendid! And now go and behold the Lotus-eyed One.
Bhattacharya. As the Lord commands. (Goes out, taking Damodara and Jagadananda with him.)
Mukunda. Why has he gone, taking those two?
Gopinatha Acharya. There is a secret in this. But, Master — is this the same Bhattacharya?
The Lord. From association with you, a great Bhagavata, he has become quite different.
Gopinatha Acharya (laughing). Just so.
(Enter hurriedly, tossing aside the curtain, Damodara and Jagadananda.)
Damodara and Jagadananda. Master! The Bhattacharya has sent two verses and alms-food — the remnants of the meal of the Lord Jagannatha.
The Lord. I am favoured.
Mukunda. Let me look at these two verses. (Taking the leaf from his hand, he reads to himself.)
notes: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.14.32 (in GGM the reference is 10.14.31).
The Sattvatas are the ancient Vaishnava Pancharatrikas. There follows an exposition of the doctrine of the vyuhas (Vasudeva, Sankarshana and so on), in which Sankarshana is called the "jiva".
Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.16.51.

verses_en.text:
That one Primeval Person who, to teach renunciation, knowledge and His own bhakti-yoga,
has assumed the body of Sri Krishna Chaitanya — the ocean of mercy: in Him I take refuge.

He who has appeared under the name of Krishna Chaitanya to reveal
His own bhakti-yoga, lost in the course of time — into His lotus feet
deeper and deeper sinks* the bee of my mind.
(Having read them, he copies them onto the wall and gives [the leaf] into the Lord's hands. The Lord, glancing at it, tears it up.)
Gopinatha Acharya. Master, it is midday. Let Your holy feet prepare for what is to be done next.
All. Just so.
(Exeunt all.)
Thus ends the sixth act of the Sri Chaitanya-chandrodaya, called "Mercy to Sarvabhauma".
*: Ratnakara ("the mine of jewels") is the Ocean, the husband of the rivers, the Ganga among them.
*: Bhagirathi is a name of the Ganga, brought down to earth by King Bhagiratha.
*: A play on words: rasa is both "moisture, water" and "taste, aesthetic feeling"; rasa-kautukī, "eager for rasa" (or "fond of water"); rasayāṁ cakāra, "relished / made me relish".
*: That is, the Lord stayed at the request of His mother and friends, and as a result His journey to Mathura (Vrindavana) was interrupted. The reading vyajani ("arose") follows the Kāvyamālā; GGM has vyajati.
*: Dhikkāra, the exclamation "shame!", reproach of themselves for letting Him go.
*: GGM has the run-together ācārio-jaṇaṇīe ("to the Acharya's mother"), which gives an unclear sense. M. Guha reads saddhaṁ ācārieṇa jaṇaṇīe (Sanskrit sārdham ācāryeṇa jananyāḥ), "together with the Acharya … to the mother"; the Acharya is Advaita. So Guha's Bengali translation and Krishnadasa Baba's Hindi translation understand the passage.
*: Shri-kshetra is Puri, the abode of Jagannatha.
*: Devahuti, the mother of the sage Kapila, let her son go to the forest after his instruction (Bhāg. 3.33). Shachi surpasses her, letting her son go for the sake of His good name.
*: Achyutananda is Advaita's son; his mother is Sita-devi, Advaita's wife.
*: The Muslim sultan of Bengal (Gauda) and the king of Orissa (Gajapati, "lord of elephants", the title of the kings of Utkala), i.e. Prataparudra.
*: According to the note of the Kāvyamālā edition, "between two kingdoms, Gauda and Utkala".
*: Paṭu-kapaṭin, "skilful cheats" (so we divide paṭukapaṭino); ghaṭṭa-pāla, toll-collectors at the crossings; vāṭa-pāṭac-cara, according to the Kāvyamālā, "highway robbers".
*: Rama, when He entered the Dandaka forest.
*: That is, the dispute is whether the worship of the two-armed Krishna with the flute (Gopinatha) is ancient, in contrast to that of the four-armed Vishnu. Remuna (near Balasore) is the site of the temple of Kshira-chora-Gopinatha.
*: Śekhara, a garland or head-ornament of the Deity.
*: Muralī-mukha, "He at whose lips is the flute", i.e. Krishna the flute-player (here the form of Gopinatha in Remuna); so M. Guha's Bengali translation ("Murali-vadana") and Krishnadasa Baba's Hindi translation ("Krishna with the flute") understand it.
*: The reading of GGM and M. Guha, -bādho labdha-srutā (in the Kāvyamālā, by the OCR, possibly -bādhoruddha-srutā). The sense according to Guha's Bengali translation: the stream of the nectar of sweetness, bursting from behind the "barrier" of the bent elbow and other joints, floods the earth, and the right arm eclipses the beauty of Krishna with the flute. Vilakṣayati literally means "puts to confusion, shames"; Guha and Krishnadasa Baba's Hindi translation render it more mildly as "reveals".
*: Mahendra is the mountains and land in the south of Utkala (Orissa).
*: So according to the Kāvyamālā and M. Guha (gajapati-mahārājena), and likewise in Krishnadasa Baba's Hindi translation; gaṅgā-pati in GGM is apparently a corruption. Gajapati ("lord of elephants") is the title of the kings of Orissa. Purushottama-deva is a fifteenth-century king of Orissa who, according to tradition, brought Sakshi-gopala from Vijayanagara (Vidyanagara) to Cuttack.
*: Akāṇḍopaplava-khaṇḍa, "a fragment of unexpected calamity"; a play daṇḍa, "staff" — "punishment" is possible. Kamalapura is a village by the river (Bhargi) near Puri.
*: The Ocean was bound by Rama's bridge and churned by the gods for the nectar; from it Lakshmi, the consort of Vishnu, was born, so the Ocean is Hari's father-in-law. Here Hari (Chaitanya) has left Lakshmi too (has accepted sannyasa) and settled on the shore of the Ocean. Taṭa-vaṭa-kuṭumbī, literally "a householder of the banyan on the shore"; M. Guha's Bengali translation understands kuṭumbī as "by right of kinship, as one of the family" (the Ocean being His father-in-law), Krishnadasa Baba's Hindi translation simply as "a dweller on my shore". Neither translation explains the banyan; probably the sacred banyan of Puri is meant.
*: Āvutta, according to the Kāvyamālā note citing the Amarakośa, "sister's husband". Visharada is the father of Sarvabhauma.
*: For a man, a throbbing of the right eye is an auspicious omen.
*: In GGM the speeches from verse 18 to this stage direction are repeated twice (an obvious typesetting error); in the Kāvyamālā, once.
*: "Namo nārāyaṇāya" is the usual greeting of Advaitin sannyasis; the Lord answers with a Vaishnava blessing, which surprises Sarvabhauma.
*: Shripada, a respectful address to a sannyasi.
*: The words in brackets are found only in the Kāvyamālā; they are missing in GGM.
*: Mahā-vākya, the "great saying" of the Upanishads (such as tat tvam asi), imparted at initiation into sannyasa.
*: Yoga-paṭṭa, the cloth or garment given at initiation into sannyasa; here, a repeated initiation in a "higher" branch of Shankara's order (the Bharatis were held lower than, for example, the Sarasvatis or Tirthas).
*: Pramāṇa, in Indian logic a means of valid knowledge (perception, inference, testimony and so on). What follows is a parody of a Nyaya disputation.
*: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.14.29 (the prayer of Brahma).
*: A brother-in-law is by custom allowed to tease his sister's husband; vyadhikaraṇa is a term of logic ("having a different substrate", i.e. "beside the point").
*: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.4.31 (Daksha's hymn "Hamsa-guhya"). The Kāvyamālā has naiṣa vo doṣaḥ, "this is not your fault"; GGM has vā.
*: Mātṛ-svasur āvāse, "in the dwelling of the mother's sister". This is Sarvabhauma's own aunt: below he says asman-mātṛ-ṣvasuḥ puram, "the house of our (my) aunt", and Krishnadasa Baba's Hindi translation likewise has "my aunt".
*: The bees are the dark pupils on the white field of Jagannatha's huge eyes.
*: The division cāru-kāruṇikam ā-rucirāṅgam, "charming (cāru = manojña), merciful (karuṇāmaya), with limbs wholly (ā-) beautiful", follows the commentary of Jivananda Vidyasagara; M. Guha's Bengali translation ("the all-merciful, captivating Daru-brahman") also sees no name of Lakshmi here. A possible other division -mā-rucira- ("beautiful with the beauty of Lakshmi") is not supported by the translations.
*: Dāru-brahman, "Brahman in wood", is Jagannatha; nara-brahman, "Brahman in a man", is Chaitanya (cf. Bhāg. 7.15.75: "the supreme Brahman hidden in human form").
*: Chaitanya is Krishna hidden within a golden form; Jagannatha is Brahman hidden in a wooden form.
*: So according to the Kāvyamālā (niḥspanda, "motionless"); GGM has niḥsyanda ("an outpouring [of bliss]").
*: In the Kāvyamālā there is a speech of Damodara here: "Master, the Acharya bows to You."
*: According to the Kāvyamālā: "Damodara, let him be invited by you."
*: Pāṇi-śaṅkha, the conch blown at dawn in the temple of Puri to awaken Jagannatha.
*: The jagamohana is the hall for pilgrims in front of the sanctuary.
*: So according to the Kāvyamālā (dīpābhāva); GGM has doṣābhāva, "[though] there is no night" (or "without fault").
*: The Gambhira/Gambhirika is the inner sanctuary of the temple.
*: The bala-bhoga is the early morning meal of Jagannatha; the Hari-vallabha is the next offering.
*: The sentence in square brackets is found only in the Kāvyamālā; without it the following speech of "Both" (Damodara and Jagadananda) hangs in the air in GGM.
*: The servants speak a vulgar Prakrit (Magadhi: ale for are, bhaṭṭācālia and so on).

*: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.14.32 (in GGM the reference is 10.14.31).
*: The Sattvatas are the ancient Vaishnava Pancharatrikas. There follows an exposition of the doctrine of the vyuhas (Vasudeva, Sankarshana and so on), in which Sankarshana is called the "jiva".
*: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.16.51.
*: Līyate, "sinks into, clings to" (of a bee in a lotus); the Kāvyamālā has līyatām, "may it sink (cling)". Verses 43–44 are quoted in the Chaitanya-charitamrita (Madhya 6.254–255).
notes: Līyate, "sinks into, clings to" (of a bee in a lotus); the Kāvyamālā has līyatām, "may it sink (cling)". Verses 43–44 are quoted in the Chaitanya-charitamrita (Madhya 6.254–255).
Ratnakara ("the mine of jewels") is the Ocean, the husband of the rivers, the Ganga among them.
Bhagirathi is a name of the Ganga, brought down to earth by King Bhagiratha.
A play on words: rasa is both "moisture, water" and "taste, aesthetic feeling"; rasa-kautukī, "eager for rasa" (or "fond of water"); rasayāṁ cakāra, "relished / made me relish".

That is, the Lord stayed at the request of His mother and friends, and as a result His journey to Mathura (Vrindavana) was interrupted. The reading vyajani ("arose") follows the Kāvyamālā; GGM has vyajati.
Dhikkāra, the exclamation "shame!", reproach of themselves for letting Him go.

GGM has the run-together ācārio-jaṇaṇīe ("to the Acharya's mother"), which gives an unclear sense. M. Guha reads saddhaṁ ācārieṇa jaṇaṇīe (Sanskrit sārdham ācāryeṇa jananyāḥ), "together with the Acharya … to the mother"; the Acharya is Advaita. So Guha's Bengali translation and Krishnadasa Baba's Hindi translation understand the passage.
Shri-kshetra is Puri, the abode of Jagannatha.
Devahuti, the mother of the sage Kapila, let her son go to the forest after his instruction (Bhāg. 3.33). Shachi surpasses her, letting her son go for the sake of His good name.
Achyutananda is Advaita's son; his mother is Sita-devi, Advaita's wife.
The Muslim sultan of Bengal (Gauda) and the king of Orissa (Gajapati, "lord of elephants", the title of the kings of Utkala), i.e. Prataparudra.
According to the note of the Kāvyamālā edition, "between two kingdoms, Gauda and Utkala".
Paṭu-kapaṭin, "skilful cheats" (so we divide paṭukapaṭino); ghaṭṭa-pāla, toll-collectors at the crossings; vāṭa-pāṭac-cara, according to the Kāvyamālā, "highway robbers".
Rama, when He entered the Dandaka forest.

That is, the dispute is whether the worship of the two-armed Krishna with the flute (Gopinatha) is ancient, in contrast to that of the four-armed Vishnu. Remuna (near Balasore) is the site of the temple of Kshira-chora-Gopinatha.
Śekhara, a garland or head-ornament of the Deity.

Muralī-mukha, "He at whose lips is the flute", i.e. Krishna the flute-player (here the form of Gopinatha in Remuna); so M. Guha's Bengali translation ("Murali-vadana") and Krishnadasa Baba's Hindi translation ("Krishna with the flute") understand it.

The reading of GGM and M. Guha, -bādho labdha-srutā (in the Kāvyamālā, by the OCR, possibly -bādhoruddha-srutā). The sense according to Guha's Bengali translation: the stream of the nectar of sweetness, bursting from behind the "barrier" of the bent elbow and other joints, floods the earth, and the right arm eclipses the beauty of Krishna with the flute. Vilakṣayati literally means "puts to confusion, shames"; Guha and Krishnadasa Baba's Hindi translation render it more mildly as "reveals".
Mahendra is the mountains and land in the south of Utkala (Orissa).

So according to the Kāvyamālā and M. Guha (gajapati-mahārājena), and likewise in Krishnadasa Baba's Hindi translation; gaṅgā-pati in GGM is apparently a corruption. Gajapati ("lord of elephants") is the title of the kings of Orissa. Purushottama-deva is a fifteenth-century king of Orissa who, according to tradition, brought Sakshi-gopala from Vijayanagara (Vidyanagara) to Cuttack.
Akāṇḍopaplava-khaṇḍa, "a fragment of unexpected calamity"; a play daṇḍa, "staff" — "punishment" is possible. Kamalapura is a village by the river (Bhargi) near Puri.

The Ocean was bound by Rama's bridge and churned by the gods for the nectar; from it Lakshmi, the consort of Vishnu, was born, so the Ocean is Hari's father-in-law. Here Hari (Chaitanya) has left Lakshmi too (has accepted sannyasa) and settled on the shore of the Ocean. Taṭa-vaṭa-kuṭumbī, literally "a householder of the banyan on the shore"; M. Guha's Bengali translation understands kuṭumbī as "by right of kinship, as one of the family" (the Ocean being His father-in-law), Krishnadasa Baba's Hindi translation simply as "a dweller on my shore". Neither translation explains the banyan; probably the sacred banyan of Puri is meant.
Āvutta, according to the Kāvyamālā note citing the Amarakośa, "sister's husband". Visharada is the father of Sarvabhauma.
For a man, a throbbing of the right eye is an auspicious omen.
In GGM the speeches from verse 18 to this stage direction are repeated twice (an obvious typesetting error); in the Kāvyamālā, once.
"Namo nārāyaṇāya" is the usual greeting of Advaitin sannyasis; the Lord answers with a Vaishnava blessing, which surprises Sarvabhauma.
Shripada, a respectful address to a sannyasi.
The words in brackets are found only in the Kāvyamālā; they are missing in GGM.
Mahā-vākya, the "great saying" of the Upanishads (such as tat tvam asi), imparted at initiation into sannyasa.

Yoga-paṭṭa, the cloth or garment given at initiation into sannyasa; here, a repeated initiation in a "higher" branch of Shankara's order (the Bharatis were held lower than, for example, the Sarasvatis or Tirthas).
Pramāṇa, in Indian logic a means of valid knowledge (perception, inference, testimony and so on). What follows is a parody of a Nyaya disputation.
Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.14.29 (the prayer of Brahma).
A brother-in-law is by custom allowed to tease his sister's husband; vyadhikaraṇa is a term of logic ("having a different substrate", i.e. "beside the point").
Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.4.31 (Daksha's hymn "Hamsa-guhya"). The Kāvyamālā has naiṣa vo doṣaḥ, "this is not your fault"; GGM has vā.

Mātṛ-svasur āvāse, "in the dwelling of the mother's sister". This is Sarvabhauma's own aunt: below he says asman-mātṛ-ṣvasuḥ puram, "the house of our (my) aunt", and Krishnadasa Baba's Hindi translation likewise has "my aunt".
The bees are the dark pupils on the white field of Jagannatha's huge eyes.

The division cāru-kāruṇikam ā-rucirāṅgam, "charming (cāru = manojña), merciful (karuṇāmaya), with limbs wholly (ā-) beautiful", follows the commentary of Jivananda Vidyasagara; M. Guha's Bengali translation ("the all-merciful, captivating Daru-brahman") also sees no name of Lakshmi here. A possible other division -mā-rucira- ("beautiful with the beauty of Lakshmi") is not supported by the translations.
Dāru-brahman, "Brahman in wood", is Jagannatha; nara-brahman, "Brahman in a man", is Chaitanya (cf. Bhāg. 7.15.75: "the supreme Brahman hidden in human form").
Chaitanya is Krishna hidden within a golden form; Jagannatha is Brahman hidden in a wooden form.
So according to the Kāvyamālā (niḥspanda, "motionless"); GGM has niḥsyanda ("an outpouring [of bliss]").
In the Kāvyamālā there is a speech of Damodara here: "Master, the Acharya bows to You."
According to the Kāvyamālā: "Damodara, let him be invited by you."
Pāṇi-śaṅkha, the conch blown at dawn in the temple of Puri to awaken Jagannatha.
The jagamohana is the hall for pilgrims in front of the sanctuary.
So according to the Kāvyamālā (dīpābhāva); GGM has doṣābhāva, "[though] there is no night" (or "without fault").
The Gambhira/Gambhirika is the inner sanctuary of the temple.
The bala-bhoga is the early morning meal of Jagannatha; the Hari-vallabha is the next offering.
The sentence in square brackets is found only in the Kāvyamālā; without it the following speech of "Both" (Damodara and Jagadananda) hangs in the air in GGM.

Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.6.
Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1.
Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3 (tad aikṣata); Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6 (so 'kāmayata).
Cf. Brahma-sūtra 1.1.24 (jyotiś caraṇābhidhānāt), where "light" is interpreted as Brahman on the ground of the mention of its "feet" (quarters).
Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.2.11. In the Kāvyamālā the verse is quoted only in part and unnumbered; in GGM in full, also unnumbered.

The construction mukhyārthābhāvābhāve 'pi is understood as "although there is no absence of the primary meaning": by the rules of poetics lakṣaṇā is resorted to only when the primary meaning is impossible, while here it is quite possible. M. Guha's Bengali translation renders the passage more freely ("both in the absence of the primary meaning and being unable to define it even by the secondary meaning"), but the general sense — a reproach of forced interpretation — is the same.
